item.title: Jensen-Bregman split Gibbs sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.15853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Split Gibbs sampling (SGS) is a versatile tool to sample from complex posterior distributions, such as those arising in imaging inverse problems. However, existing SGS instances are limited to quadratic variable couplings, restricting their applicability to Gaussian likelihoods. This letter genearalizes SGS to non-Euclidean geometry by introducing a coupling kernel defined through a Jensen-Bregman divergence. This framework not only enables posterior sampling in these settings but also unifies several \emph{ad hoc} sampling schemes from the literature under a principled theoretical foundation.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Dobigeon, Mame Diarra Fall, Eric Barat

item.title: Locally adaptive step sizes for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.16506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact reversible locally adaptive step sizes are introduced by Bou-Rabee et al. (2026) in the context of the No-U-Turn Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampler for the purpose of high performance HMC sampling in challenging target distributions. This paper carefully explains and illustrates the locally adaptive step size procedure under more general assumptions. Alternative error measures are introduced with the aim of further enhancing MCMC performance by reducing the prevalence of reversibility failure rejections. In addition, the paper shows how to introduce the locally adaptive step sizes also within standard HMC and Metropolis-corrected kinetic Langevin/generalized HMC (GHMC). Finally, a numerical study of the relative merits of the proposed error measures in the context of different Hamiltonian flow-based MCMC methods is provided.
item.dc:creator: Jimmy Huy Tran, Tore Selland Kleppe, Nawaf Bou-Rabee

item.title: A hybrid GPU/CPU implementation of the average information restricted maximum likelihood algorithm for fitting multivariate linear mixed models
item.description: arXiv:2610.16671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The multivariate linear mixed model combined with restricted maximum likelihood estimation of (co)variance components and solving the mixed model equations is widely used for the analysis of plant breeding data. Several algorithms for restricted maximum likelihood estimation have been proposed, with the average information algorithm being widely used for its computational efficiency, quadratic rate of convergence, and ability to handle large amounts of parameters. A key reason for the scalability of linear mixed models is the exploitation of sparse matrix techniques. Recently, decreasing costs of high-throughput data collection have led to high-dimensional sets of features characterizing genotypes and environments. A convenient way of using these features is through the use of kernel-based covariance structures. However, while convenient, these kernels typically have dense inverses meaning optimizations based on sparse matrix techniques are not always applicable. For these settings, the introduction of general-purpose computing on graphics processing units brought significant computational advantages for dense linear algebra operations. We present a hybrid GPU/CPU implementation of the average information restricted maximum likelihood algorithm. We eliminate sparse equations using supernodal Cholesky factorization and rely on CUDA GPU acceleration to solve the resulting reduced dense system. We show the significant computational advantages of this approach for fully dense problems, as well as problems with a mix of dense and sparse equations.
item.dc:creator: Killian A. C. Melsen, Fred A. van Eeuwijk, Carel F. W. Peeters

item.title: CLASSO: a practical primal path-following algorithm for the constrained LASSO
item.description: arXiv:2610.17024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present CLASSO, a path-following method for the LASSO subject to general linear equality and inequality constraints. The local direction is obtained from a quadratic programme on an augmented active set, which determines both the coefficients that leave zero and the weakly active inequalities that remain binding. For a positive-definite Hessian and a nonempty feasible set, this programme has a unique primal minimiser, even when the binding constraint rows are dependent, and gives the local derivative of the solution path. The construction recovers the LASSO-modified LARS direction without constraints, and over the full cone gives the segment leaving the origin. We prove that the primal path is piecewise affine with finitely many kinks, without a constraint qualification or unique multipliers. A finite path does not imply a finite traversal: re-certifying at each kink can fail to terminate. CLASSO instead follows the minimum-norm certificate along a lexicographic rate; we prove that this rule reaches $\lambda=0$ in exact arithmetic within an explicit bound and traverses the whole path. These results are machine-checked in Lean~4, and the floating-point implementation agrees with an exact rational one on all $210$ small test problems. We assess the implementation on a $39$-case synthetic suite and six constrained versions of the diabetes benchmark. On the $31$ nontrivial synthetic cases with $n\ge p$, sampled relative objective differences from numerical reference solves are below $10^{-9}$ in magnitude; unnormalised endpoint differences reach $1.5\times10^{-7}$ in magnitude. For $n<p$, matched differences range from $-3.6\times10^{-7}$ to $2\times10^{-9}$ across five ridge strengths. Across the synthetic and diabetes benchmarks, checks of all $580$ recorded segments found no missed interior event and all checked KKT residuals within the stated tolerances.
item.dc:creator: Michael Hobson, Luke Butcher, Lindley Lentati

item.title: Overlap, Not Moments: Finite-Sample Theory for Bridge Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.17403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bridge sampling estimates of marginal likelihoods are routinely reported with a delta-method Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE). Existing theory is asymptotic and cannot say whether a given run is long enough to trust the estimate or its MCSE. We give finite-sample answers. The optimal bridge estimator fits a logistic regression that separates posterior from proposal draws, and its accuracy is governed by their overlap, within a factor of two of the classification's Bayes error. Because the estimating function is a sum of bounded terms, no moment conditions are needed, and all bounds hold uniformly over targets, proposals and dimensions. A number of draws inversely proportional to the overlap suffices and is necessary in the worst case, paralleling the exponential-in-Kullback--Leibler requirement of importance sampling. A Berry--Esseen bound with an explicit constant holds at the optimal rate, and the MCSE is accurate once the effective overlap is large; it is estimated at no cost. For Markov chain draws, the required sample size grows in proportion to the sampler's relaxation time, unavoidably in the worst case. The estimated bridge, the fixed-point iteration and the fitted proposal matter only at second order, and we give free diagnostics for sampler failure and misestimated autocorrelation.
item.dc:creator: Giorgio Micaletto

item.title: How to Train Your Intercept: A Comparison of Intercept Update Strategies in Coordinate Descent
item.description: arXiv:2610.18043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coordinate descent solvers for regularized generalized linear models (GLMs) differ in how they update the intercept. This seemingly routine choice can substantially affect convergence when the response is imbalanced. For direct coordinate descent on the original GLM loss, we compare a conservative step based on worst-case curvature, a safeguarded Newton step based on current curvature, and repeated Newton steps that solve the intercept subproblem. The conservative update can leave much of the interaction between the intercept and the coefficients unresolved, producing a slowdown when that interaction controls convergence. A single Newton step avoids this attenuation and, in our experiments, follows nearly the same outer trajectory as exact minimization while requiring fewer inner steps. Simulated and real-data experiments, including comparisons across six production solvers and a controlled intervention within skglm, support this explanation. We also show how the same mechanism appears in quadratic-approximation methods and extends to multinomial models with rare classes. We recommend a safeguarded Newton update for direct coordinate descent and full intercept optimization within frozen local quadratic surrogates.
item.dc:creator: Johan Larsson, Frederik Fabricius-Bjerre

item.title: Rapid Mixing of Stereographic MCMC for Heavy-Tailed Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.18513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sampling from high-dimensional, heavy-tailed distributions is a fundamental challenge in computational statistics, as many standard Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods mix poorly in such settings. Recently, Stereographic MCMC [Yang et al., 2024] and the Sub-Cauchy Projection Sampler [Grazzi et al., 2026] have been shown to perform successfully on such tasks. However, establishing their non-asymptotic convergence properties remains an important open problem. In this work, we fill this gap by establishing non-asymptotic upper bounds on the mixing time of the stereographic projection and sub-Cauchy projection samplers. Our results demonstrate that, under certain conditions on the target and initial distributions, the mixing time is polynomial in dimension for a broad class of distributions, including light- and heavy-tailed cases. Motivated by the theoretical analysis, we further establish a new weighted isoperimetric inequality that extends the classical version for log-concave distributions to the heavy-tailed setting with optimal dimension dependence. The proof techniques provide new insights into the geometric properties of heavy-tailed distributions that govern rapid mixing in high dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Federica Milinanni, Tyler Farghly, Jun Yang

item.title: cvxoptdes: convex optimal experiment design in R
item.description: arXiv:2610.14288v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The cvxoptdes R-package provides a unified framework to perform convex optimal experiment design and online response optimization for linear, generalized linear and additive, nonlinear, and random intercept mixed models, using exclusively open-source solvers. It supports optimization and augmentation of weighted, penalized and convex constrained continuous designs across a discrete grid of candidate points and rounding to integer-valued designs using point-exchange algorithms or mixed-integer programming for orthogonally constrained designs, including the class of orthogonal minimally aliased response surface (OMARS) designs. Models and design constraints are defined and updated in an object-oriented context with the aim to facilitate the process of sequential (penalized) design augmentation analogous to online design procedures known from active learning and Bayesian optimization.
item.dc:creator: Joris Chau, Alexandre Segers, Martin Otava, Stephen Karanja

item.title: Copula Active Subspaces II: Error Decomposition, A Posteriori Estimation, and Sharpness of the Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.14498v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Copula Active Subspaces (CAS) method of Part I estimates a non-Gaussian observation-noise density $\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}}$ from residual samples. Its KL divergence $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}}\,\|\,\widehat\pi_{\boldsymbol{n}})$ admits an exact decomposition into marginal, projection and reduced-density terms and bounds the posterior KL divergence averaged over the true predictive distribution. We derive a priori bounds for these terms, together with estimates or bounds from residual samples. Weighted nearest-neighbour entropy estimates are used for the marginal and reduced-density terms, with asymptotic standard errors in exact rank coordinates. For the projection error, the score is fitted on one subsample, and its mean squared magnitude outside the retained subspace is estimated on the other. Corrections for score and rank-transform errors then give a theoretical upper bound with probability at least $1-\delta$. Tests on three known noise laws in dimension $d=20$ use the estimated rank transform. In $11$ of $12$ combinations of example and sample size, the sum of the two estimated terms and the trace bound exceeds the reference divergence after averaging over the estimated models. In these tests, score-estimation error is the largest contribution to looseness. The overestimate from the Gaussian log-Sobolev inequality alone is at most a factor of $1.98$.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Chen, Peter Jan van Leeuwen

item.title: Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification of Breast-Cancer Pathology AI Agreement under Reader- and Annotation-Condition-Dependent Reference Labels
item.description: arXiv:2610.14642v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Human reference labels used to evaluate medical AI can vary across readers and annotation workflows. We quantified agreement of a fixed pathology AI system with a future qualified reader without treating inferred consensus as error-free biological truth. Linked Evaluation and Unbiased NuCLS multirater data were analyzed using a fixed external HoVer-Net decision vector. The selected frame contained 1,144 anchors, 52 fields of view, five slides/patients, and five primary readers. The target was fixed-AI agreement with a future reader, with descriptive contrast $\Delta=\theta_E-\theta_U$. Analyses included raw agreement and iMRMC benchmarks, reader-only and shared-detectability Bayesian models, structural sensitivities, adversarial simulations, and predictive assessment. Among 5,188 reader-anchor pairs observed in both conditions, 19.62% changed AI-agreement state, while raw agreement was 0.5466 in Unbiased and 0.5473 in Evaluation. The reader-only model gave $\Delta=-0.0008$ (95% CrI, $-0.0033$ to $0.0008$), and the shared-detectability model gave $\Delta\approx0$ ($-0.0140$ to $0.0127$). Across structural perturbations, absolute agreement ranged from 0.420 to 0.646 in Unbiased and 0.409 to 0.640 in Evaluation. Frozen adversarial simulations met the comparative-stability criterion (median $R=0.295$; 14/16 model-scenario cells had $R<1$). Held-out-AI prediction supported shared predictive information, but varied by slide composition. The Evaluation-minus-Unbiased contrast was comparatively stable, whereas absolute agreement was structurally sensitive. These findings do not establish equivalence, causal assistance effects, biological accuracy, or new-patient transportability. Evaluations using variable human references should report reader population, selected frame, observation mechanism, and structural sensitivity.
item.dc:creator: Hammed A. Olayinka

item.title: An Algebraic Approach to Constrained K-means Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2610.14932v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clustering is typically performed using only object features, although additional information about relationships between objects may be available and can be incorporated through constraints. Among these, pairwise constraints require two objects to belong to the same cluster or to different clusters. Several extensions of the k-means algorithm accommodate such constraints, but they sometimes fail to find a feasible assignment or incur high computational cost. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an algebraic approach to k-means clustering with pairwise constraints. The algorithm simplifies the constraints using Gr\"{o}bner bases before optimization, improving the efficiency of cluster assignment. It can also detect whether the constraint set has a feasible assignment before optimization. Comparative experiments with existing algorithms showed that the proposed algorithm achieved comparable or better clustering quality at a lower computational cost, particularly when the numbers of constraints and clusters were small.
item.dc:creator: Hiroki Oohori, Kentaro Fukushima, Michio Yamamoto

item.title: Approximation, Consistency, and Prediction in Generalized Neural Network Mixed Models for Longitudinal and Clustered Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.15270v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generalized neural network mixed models (GNMMs) combine neural networks and mixed-effects models to analyze longitudinal and clustered data. Although GNMMs have shown good predictive performance in practice, their statistical properties are not well understood. Therefore, this paper studies several important properties of GNMM and provides theoretical support for its use. First, we show that the neural-network component can approximate an unknown nonlinear fixed-effect function arbitrarily well and establish consistency of the fitted neural- network function for its population target within a given network class. Next, we establish consistency of random-effect estimation under increasing within-subject information and show that the GNMM predictor converges to the true predictor. We then prove consistency of the conditional mean function and show that the excess mean squared prediction error (MSPE) relative to the oracle prediction error converges to zero. We conduct simulation studies to examine nonlinear fixed-effect recovery, random-effect estimation, predictor and conditional mean estimation, and excess prediction error under different numbers of subjects and repeated observations. We also apply GNMM to a longitudinal schizophrenia dataset to predict continuous and binary depression outcomes using smartphone- based behavioral measurements and compare its predictive performance with generalized linear mixed models and conventional artificial neural networks. Both the theoretical and empirical results demonstrate that GNMM provides a flexible framework for modeling nonlinear longitudinal and clustered data. These findings provide a statistical foundation for GNMM prediction and support future methodological developments.
item.dc:creator: Mahmud Hasan, Md Moinul Ahsan, Mathias Nthiani Muia, Mous-Abou Hamadou, Chathurika S Abeykoon

item.title: Imperfect Verifiers, Exact Targets: Inference-Time Scaling for Continuous Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.15281v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Verifier-guided inference-time scaling uses additional computation to score intermediate states and steer generation toward better outputs. However, imperfect intermediate verifiers can distort sampling, and repeated refinement alone does not ensure recovery of the desired reward-tilted distribution. We introduce Continuous-State Verifier-Guided Backtracking (CS-VGB), an inference-time scaling method for sampling from reward-tilted distributions with continuous generative models through repeated denoising and renoising. With correctly paired denoising and renoising transitions, the stationary distribution of CS-VGB at the clean checkpoint equals the desired reward-tilted target, even when intermediate verifiers are inaccurate. Under stated regularity conditions, CS-VGB converges exponentially to the target despite verifier error, and the expected number of updates needed to reach a clean sample grows only linearly with the number of checkpoints. In analytically tractable settings, we empirically demonstrate that CS-VGB recovers the desired reward-tilted distribution despite verifier error, whereas the compared verifier-based sampling methods fail to recover the target under the same verifier errors. We also instantiate the framework with diffusion models and one-step stochastic posterior maps. Across prompt-guided ImageNet generation, facial-attribute generation on CelebA, and multi-robot planning, recurrent CS-VGB search improves reward and task success as inference budgets grow, with image-generation rewards continuing beyond the observed plateaus of denoising-only baselines.
item.dc:creator: Kijung Jeon, Molei Tao

item.title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2610.16187v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing cumulative regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization (BO) do not necessarily characterize the quality of the algorithm's final output. This gap is critical under noisy evaluations, where the goal is to return a single high-quality recommendation. To address it, we introduce efficient exploration strategies that can be incorporated into any BO procedure by occasionally replacing the acquisition query with an exploration query. To validate this approach, we bound the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, which measures the largest region left unexplored. We then use this result to derive upper bounds on the inference regret, i.e., the gap between the global optimum and the function value at the algorithm's returned point. Empirically, these exploration strategies improve the final recommendations of existing BO algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.
item.dc:creator: Hwanwoo Kim, Jungwoo Hong, Kyungjae Lee

item.title: Optimal Monte Carlo integration on matrix manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2610.16965v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This article develops optimal order (up to logarithmic factors) weighted cubature rules for Monte Carlo numerical integration in Sobolev reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces over common matrix manifolds. Specifically, we consider matrix models of the Stiefel, Grassmann, flag, and Lagrangian Grassmann manifolds each over either real numbers $\mathbb{R}$, complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$, or quaternions $\mathbb{H}$. The proposed cubature rules use evaluation points which are independent and identically distributed uniform on the manifold. The weights are chosen to be optimal with respect to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space worst-case error, under the constraint that the weights sum to one. Crucially, this constraint ensures optimal weights may be found without having to evaluate the kernel mean embedding (the integral of the kernel), which is often difficult to compute. We consider computable Mat\'ern kernels of Frobenius distances between matrices which reproduce the Sobolev reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces with equivalent norms. Open-source numerical experiments validate our theoretical development, including an application to simultaneous approximation of intrinsic volumes in the Cauchy--Kubota formula. We also present preliminary empirical results beyond independent points including transformations of low-discrepancy quasi-Monte Carlo points from the unit cube and jointly optimized points and weights.
item.dc:creator: Aleksei G. Sorokin, Yihan Guo, Lek-Heng Lim

item.title: The hypervariational method: a general, automated technique based on innovations to tune the parameters of the Hybrid covariance matrix
item.description: arXiv:2610.17561v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Hybrid forecast covariance model is an operationally successful way to build a background error covariance matrix. It is constructed as a weighted sum, with scalar weights, of the climatological covariance matrix and a localized ensemble covariance matrix, with a localization matrix typically depending on a localization length. For best performance, the Hybrid needs to be optimized by tuning those weights and, possibly, other parameters, such as the localization length. Here, a systematic and automated method for this tuning operation is introduced. This technique is referred to as hypervariational method, and it is formulated in terms of a cost function, built using a time series of innovations as an essential ingredient. This cost function, which depends on the parameters, is minimized when they have optimal values. Equations for its minimization, based on Newton's method, are derived. Besides the aforementioned, commonly used Hybrid, the hypervariational method is applicable to any known Hybrid (and to any set of parameters on which it depends analytically), including recently developed Hybrids, not necessarily constructed as weighted sums. Here, the hypervariational method is applied to tune the ensemble covariance matrix weight in the seminal-formulation Hybrid (which does not feature localization). This is done in a synthetic experimental setting where a theoretically-derived expression for the optimal value for that weight is known. Moreover, in that experimental setting, a further method, based on a linear fit procedure, to determine that optimal value is possible. Both the hypervariational method and that linear fit procedure are shown to produce an optimal weight value matching (up to a tolerance of $0.1$) the optimal value known from the theory. Furthermore, Newton's minimization in the hypervariational method is shown to converge immediately (at the first recursive step).
item.dc:creator: Francesco Sardelli (School of Geography, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Melbourne, Australia), Craig H. Bishop (School of Geography, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Melbourne, Australia, Bureau of Meteorology, Australia)

item.title: Free-support Wasserstein Resampling in Sequential Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2610.17924v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In modern sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) applications, such as diffusion model samplers, propagating a particle is expensive, so only a few particles can be afforded. In this regime, each resampling step decides which regions of the state space survive, so a better resampling scheme is worth extra computation. However, classical resampling methods only replicate existing particles and suffer from sample impoverishment, especially when the particle size is small relative to the dimension. To create new particles, we relax the unbiasedness of resampling and control the mean squared error via a Wasserstein criterion. Specifically, we propose Wasserstein-Dirichlet resampling (WDR), which constructs an equal-weight measure that optimally approximates the weighted particle distribution by solving a free-support Wasserstein barycenter problem. We then randomize the resulting optimal coupling by Dirichlet mixing. Theoretically, we provide non-asymptotic mean squared error bounds that quantify the bias-variance trade-off and show that the rate depends on the intrinsic dimension. A truncated variant preserves high-weight particles while applying WDR to the remaining mass, targeting mild weight degeneracy. Experiments on state-space models and conditional image generation demonstrate that WDR consistently improves estimation accuracy, stability, and sample diversity. The improvements persist at matched wall-clock cost when the propagation cost dominates.
item.dc:creator: Mengyu Li, Cheng Meng, Jun S. Liu

item.title: Optimal scaling and curvature correction for constrained MCMC on spheres
item.description: arXiv:2610.17946v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sampling Gaussian measures restricted to nonlinear manifolds in high dimensions requires a proposal kernel that respects both geometric constraints and dimensional scaling requirements. We introduce tangent preconditioned Crank-Nicolson (pCN), which combines a manifold projection with a cancellation of the ambient Gaussian contribution, leaving only a geometric residual. Considering a shifted sphere with $\sqrt d$ scaling of radius and centre as a tractable benchmark embedded manifold, we prove that uncorrected tangent pCN results in a proposal noise scale of order $d^{-1/6}$ (compared to $d^{-1/2}$ for a tangent random-walk). We establish asymptotic optimal tuning for the geodesic expected squared jump distance which is maximised at an acceptance probability of 0.574 for the family of drift-corrected tangent proposals containing tangent pCN and tangent MALA. We also prove a joint diffusion limit for the parallel and orthogonal coordinates to the sphere's centre vector of tangent pCN. The orthogonal diffusion speed matches the limiting geodesic expected squared jump distance and is maximised at acceptance probability 0.574, whereas the parallel speed is maximised at 0.712, demonstrating that optimal tuning depends on the observable. We then identify an intrinsic precision correction characterised by potential Hessian and Ricci curvature that yields a proposal kernel with dimension-independent fixed step size limit. We discuss a generalisation to arbitrary hypersurfaces and present nondegenerate scaling of tangent pCN applied to conditioned diffusions under resolution refinement.
item.dc:creator: Nayef Shkeir, Tobias Grafke

item.title: A Randomized Approximation Algorithm for Doubly Free-Boundary Macdonald Processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.18698v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We construct an approximate sampler for finite doubly free-boundary Macdonald rail-yard processes with Macdonald, boundary, and edge parameters in $(0,1)$. The construction allows arbitrary finite sequences of additions and removals of horizontal or vertical strips and all four boundary types. It reverses a finite commutation--reflection history from a partition sequence whose entries are equal, with the common partition weighted by both boundaries. We derive local reconstruction kernels from the skew Cauchy, Littlewood, and branching identities. Bulk and boundary updates combine integer increments with conditional shape sampling at a prescribed size; same-sign swaps use finite conditional resampling. For $K$ reflection periods and an initial partition-size cutoff $M$, the algorithm terminates almost surely and samples the resulting approximating law exactly. We prove total variation convergence to the target process as $K,M\to\infty$ and give explicit bounds for both truncation errors, decaying geometrically in the cutoffs for fixed input parameters. Under fixed parameter bounds, we also bound the expected operation count of direct enumeration in a unit-cost model. We further construct an exact rejection sampler for the initial partition law without a size cutoff or evaluation of its normalizing constant. Using this sampler removes the size-truncation error, leaving only the error from the finite reflection history.
item.dc:creator: Zhongyang Li

item.title: Sampling with collective variables: Relative error analysis for umbrella sampling under general conditions
item.description: arXiv:2610.18717v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the expectation of a function (observable) with respect to a high-dimensional probability distribution, under the assumption that a low-dimensional collective variable map captures all the directions of slow mixing for the distribution. More precisely, under the assumption that the fibers of the collective variable map satisfy a log-Sobolev inequality, we establish non-asymptotic relative-error guarantees for this problem using the eigenvector method for umbrella sampling (EMUS). Our analysis applies to both log-Lipschitz observables and indicator of convex sets, and gives complexity bounds that are polynomial in regularity parameters and inverse relative accuracy, and exponential in the dimension of the collective variable space. As a relative error guarantee, our bounds apply to rare event estimation. We consider Gaussian biasing windows defined on a low-dimensional collective variable space and analyze a modified sparse matrix version of EMUS. The bounds quantify the effect of the map through mixing of the conditional distribution and fluctuation of the observable along the fibers.
item.dc:creator: Holden Lee, Matheau Santana-Gijzen, Jonathan Weare

item.title: Noisy Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for doubly-intractable distributions
item.description: arXiv:1706.10096v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) has been progressively incorporated within the statistician's toolbox as an alternative sampling method in settings when standard Metropolis-Hastings is inefficient. HMC generates a Markov chain on an augmented state space with transitions based on a deterministic differential flow derived from Hamiltonian mechanics. In practice, the evolution of Hamiltonian systems cannot be solved analytically, requiring numerical integration schemes. Under numerical integration, the resulting approximate solution no longer preserves the measure of the target distribution, therefore an accept-reject step is used to correct the bias. For doubly-intractable distributions -- such as posterior distributions based on Gibbs random fields -- HMC suffers from some computational difficulties: computation of gradients in the differential flow and computation of the accept-reject proposals poses difficulty. In this paper, we study the behaviour of HMC when these quantities are replaced by Monte Carlo estimates.
item.dc:creator: Julien Stoehr, Alan Benson, Nial Friel

item.title: An Infinite BART model
item.description: arXiv:2511.20087v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) is a popular Bayesian ensemble model used in regression and classification analysis. Under this modeling framework, the regression function is approximated by an ensemble of decision trees, interpreted as weak learners. In this work, we propose a generalization of the BART model that has two main features: first, it automatically selects the number of decision trees using the given data; second, the model allows clusters of observations to have different regression functions since each data point can only use a selection of weak learners, instead of all of them. This model generalization is accomplished by including a binary weight matrix in the conditional distribution of the response variable, which activates only a specific subset of decision trees for each observation. Such a matrix is endowed with an Indian Buffet process prior, and sampled within the MCMC sampler, together with the other BART parameters. We then compare the Infinite BART model with the classic one on simulated and real datasets. Specifically, we provide examples illustrating variable importance, partial dependence and causal estimation.
item.dc:creator: Marco Battiston, Yu Luo

item.title: Kernelized Stein Discrepancy for Goodness-of-Fit Tests and Stein Sampling in R
item.description: arXiv:2608.26450v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stein's method constructs computable discrepancies between a target distribution and a candidate distribution without requiring the target distribution's normalizing constant. These discrepancies support goodness-of-fit tests for model assessment as well as sampling tools for empirical approximation. The R package steinsampling provides the first unified R workflow for applying score-based Stein methods to kernel goodness-of-fit testing of independent or serially dependent observations, point transport, greedy point construction, and sample compression. High-level functions carry out each task in a single call, while the kernel, calibration, optimization, and transition components are provided separately so that users can replace any one of them. A single score and kernel setup can therefore be reused across sampling and testing, making these methods easier to reproduce, compare, and extend.
item.dc:creator: Junhao Gao, Ery Arias-Castro

item.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Thompson Sampling for Multi-Armed Bandits
item.description: arXiv:1808.02932v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In stochastic multi-armed bandits, rewards are generated by an unknown distribution; the world's reward uncertainty induces the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Thompson sampling (TS) addresses this trade-off elegantly, but requires knowing the reward model's parametric form to sample from its posterior and compute per-arm expected rewards ---which limits its applicability as it demands per-scenario model specification and hyperparameter tuning. We here adopt Bayesian nonparametric (BNP) mixture models to remove this requirement, extending TS to arbitrary reward distributions. We model each arm's unknown reward distribution with an independent BNP Gaussian mixture, which can approximate any continuous reward density, and adapts its complexity to sequentially observed data. Embedding the BNP mixture model into TS yields Nonparametric TS, an algorithm that sequentially learns the reward model that best approximates the true, yet unknown, per-arm reward distribution, avoiding case-by-case model specification and hyperparameter tuning. We empirically demonstrate that ($i$) Nonparametric TS matches the regret performance of Oracle TS policies that know the true reward model; ($ii$) it favorably compares (in cumulative regret and volatility) to a suite of state-of-the-art alternatives across multimodal, outlier-contaminated, and non-exponential-family reward distributions; and ($iii$) its Bayesian nonparametric inference remains computationally practical and accurate for regret minimization.
item.dc:creator: I\~nigo Urteaga, Chris H. Wiggins

item.title: Sublinear Algorithms for Wasserstein and Total Variation Distances: Applications to Fairness and Privacy Auditing
item.description: arXiv:2503.07775v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Resource-efficiently computing representations of probability distributions and the distances between them while only having access to the samples is a fundamental and useful problem across mathematical sciences. In this paper, we propose a generic framework to learn the probability and cumulative distribution functions (PDFs and CDFs) of a sub-Weibull, i.e. almost any light- or heavy-tailed, distribution while the samples from it arrive in a stream. The idea is to reduce these problems into estimating the frequency of an appropriately chosen subset of the support of a properly discretised distribution. We leverage this reduction to compute mergeable summaries of distributions from the stream of samples while requiring only sublinear space relative to the number of observed samples. This allows us to estimate Wasserstein and Total Variation (TV) distances between any two distributions while samples arrive in streams and from multiple sources. Our algorithms significantly improves on the existing methods for distance estimation incurring super-linear time and linear space complexities, and further extend the mergeable summaries framework to continuous distributions with possibly infinite support. Our results are tight with respect to the existing lower bounds for bounded discrete distributions. In addition, we leverage our proposed estimators of Wasserstein and TV distances to tightly audit the fairness and privacy of algorithms. We empirically demonstrate the efficiency of proposed algorithms across synthetic and real-world datasets.
item.dc:creator: Debabrota Basu, Debarshi Chanda

item.title: Sampling from multimodal distributions with warm starts: Non-asymptotic bounds for the Reweighted Annealed Leap-Point Sampler
item.description: arXiv:2512.17977v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sampling from multimodal distributions is a central challenge in Bayesian inference and machine learning. In light of hardness results for sampling -- classical MCMC methods, even with tempering, can suffer from exponential mixing times -- a natural question is how to leverage additional information, such as a warm start point for each mode, to enable faster mixing across modes. To address this, we introduce Reweighted ALPS (Re-ALPS), a modified version of the Annealed Leap-Point Sampler (ALPS) that dispenses with the Gaussian approximation assumption. We prove the first polynomial-time bound that works in a general setting, under a natural assumption that each component contains significant mass relative to the others when tilted towards the corresponding warm start point. Similarly to ALPS, we define distributions tilted towards a mixture centered at the warm start points, and at the coldest level, use teleportation between warm start points to enable efficient mixing across modes. In contrast to ALPS, our method does not require Hessian information at the modes, but instead estimates component partition functions via Monte Carlo. This additional estimation step is crucial in allowing the algorithm to handle target distributions with more complex geometries besides approximate Gaussian. For the proof, we show convergence results for Markov processes when only part of the stationary distribution is well-mixing and estimation for partition functions for individual components of a mixture.
item.dc:creator: Holden Lee, Matheau Santana-Gijzen

item.title: Risk Control of Traffic Flow Through Chance Constraints and Large Deviation Approximation
item.description: arXiv:2604.01321v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a rare chance-constrained optimal control framework for autonomous traffic management, with traffic dynamics governed by stochastic partial differential equations. To efficiently enforce these probabilistic safety specifications, we exploit a large deviation theory (LDT) based approximation method, which converts the original highly non-convex, sampling-heavy stochastic optimization problem into a tractable deterministic nonlinear programming problem. The proposed LDT-based reformulation exhibits superior computational scalability, as its computational cost remains approximately constant regardless of the target violation probability, as opposed to the scaling challenge of traditional sampling-based methods. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is illustrated through numerical experiments on a ring road with stochastic on-ramp inflow, and evaluated with two representative risk measures, namely, maximum traffic density and speed variation. The results show that the proposed method keeps the violation probability close to the target without parameter tuning and is more than ten times faster than a risk-averse baseline.
item.dc:creator: Rui Xu, Shanyin Tong, Xuan Di

item.title: Stabilised weighted data subsampling for accelerated Bayesian inference in models with recursive likelihoods
item.description: arXiv:2605.13397v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bayesian inference for models with recursively defined likelihoods is computationally demanding, limiting scalability to large datasets. We propose a stabilised weighted subsampling methodology for accelerated Bayesian inference based on an unbiased estimator of the log-likelihood. By assigning higher sampling probabilities to early observations, the method reduces the effective depth of recursive likelihood evaluations and hence computational cost. This creates a challenging variance-cost trade-off: sampling probabilities that decay too slowly yield limited computational savings, while overly aggressive decay can substantially inflate estimator variance. We develop a stabilisation framework, supported by theory, that controls this trade-off and leads to a practical, theory-informed tuning strategy. We also derive an unbiased subsampling estimator of the log-likelihood gradient, enabling gradient-based Bayesian inference. The methodology can be embedded within a range of Bayesian computational algorithms. We illustrate its use in variational Bayes and subsampling Markov chain Monte Carlo for conditional volatility models, including leverage effects. Empirical results show substantial computational speed-ups relative to full-data methods while maintaining inferential accuracy. We also compare with recent stochastic gradient MCMC and divide-and-conquer MCMC methods for temporally dependent data, observing favourable empirical performance.
item.dc:creator: Matias Quiroz, Aishwarya Bhaskaran, Zixuan Wang, Thomas Goodwin

item.title: A stable method for direct estimation of single-index terms in GAMs with an application to bike-sharing demand
item.description: arXiv:2605.21641v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Single-index terms have been increasingly applied in generalized additive models (GAMs) across diverse areas due to their versatility in integrating functional flexibility with parametric dimension reduction while maintaining interpretability. However, the estimation presents severe computational challenges. This paper introduces a stable method based on Fisher scoring that dynamically updates the boundaries of the single-index covariates within a unified iterative framework using P-splines. Simulation studies with moderate sample sizes under non-Gaussian distributions confirm the empirical consistency of the estimation across multiple scenarios. Notably, the proposed method remains stable where state-of-the-art competitive methods fail to recover true single-index coefficients and their associated nonlinear functions, and is 80.13 times faster than the usual two-step method in the most computationally intensive scenario. The modeling advantage is illustrated through an application to Capital Bike Sharing data, where we deal with a single-index interaction effect for each year, with distinct single-index coefficients, a complex structure that makes competitive methods inapplicable. The proposed method is implemented in R, with all functions available at https://github.com/silva-danilo/sipgam for reproducibility and transparency in comparisons.
item.dc:creator: Danilo V. Silva, Gilberto A. Paula

item.title: GRACE: A General, Exact Changepoint Calculus
item.description: arXiv:2609.28831v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce GRACE (the General Regime-Aware Changepoint Estimator), a general, globally exact multiple-changepoint detection and estimation framework in which arbitrary numbers of model parameters may change at or persist across estimated changepoint locations, and all permissible changepoint types and patterns of parameter sharing compete within a single $\ell_0$-penalized optimization. The analyst specifies which types of changepoints are permitted and which parameters each type must preserve, without specifying which changes actually occur, where they occur, or in what order. GRACE jointly estimates the number and locations of changepoints, the type of change at each location, the model fitted between changepoints, and all continuous parameters. As a direct consequence, GRACE can estimate models in which the slope persists across a mean shift. The generality of the framework is achieved through an exact dynamic-programming recursion that retains the accumulated fitting cost conditional on whichever parameters a subsequent change may preserve, tracking multiple parameters jointly when necessary. We establish the global exactness of the recursion and develop functional, penalty-based, and objective-bound pruning rules that eliminate candidates without sacrificing optimality. Ordinary optimal partitioning, FPOP, and CPOP are recovered as special cases, while piecewise-polynomial and seasonal models illustrate the broader range of permissible segment structures and transitions. The resulting framework supports heterogeneous changepoint types, parameter sharing across segments, and substantial parallel computation within a unified approach to exact changepoint estimation.
item.dc:creator: Michael Grantham
